title: Human rabies exposure cases on the rise, CDC warns - KSN.com

analysis.time: The CDC issued a new alert on Thursday, with additional cases reported across July and August 2026. A rabies-infected bat was found in Yosemite earlier this year, and a bat in Raleigh, North Carolina, tested positive in late 2026. The CDC also paused diagnostic testing for rabies earlier this year but resumed it by early September 2026.
analysis.location_and_population: The CDC's advisory applies to healthcare providers nationwide, with specific mentions of Suffolk, Virginia; Mire, Louisiana; Elmira, New York; and Yosemite and Raleigh, North Carolina. The CDC reports that nearly 300 people in the state were exposed to rabies via a mobile petting zoo’s baby goats, and the agency notes that rabies is not uncommon in the U.S.
analysis.event: The CDC warned of an increase in reported cases of human exposure to rabid or possibly rabid animals, and errors in the administration of responsive care. Health officials in Suffolk, Virginia, and Mire, Louisiana, also issued local warnings about rabies-positive animals. In Elmira, New York, multiple cats and skunks tested positive for the virus.
analysis.scale_impact_and_risk: The CDC reported a 17% increase in rabies-related inquiries compared to the same time in 2025. Rabies vaccines and immunoglobulins usage is up 33% and 76%, respectively. The CDC emphasized the importance of rabies post-exposure prophylaxis (PEP) to prevent the virus from spreading to the central nervous system, as symptoms can begin with flu-like illnesses and progress to severe disease within weeks or months.
analysis.response_status_and_uncertainty: The CDC encouraged healthcare providers to adhere to PEP and other rabies guidance. Health officials advised keeping pets up to date on rabies vaccines and avoiding contact with wildlife, especially those that are injured, sick, or dead. The CDC also warned that death is inevitable once symptoms appear, but PEP can prevent this.

analysis.brief_en: The CDC has issued a new alert warning of an increase in reported cases of human exposure to rabid or possibly rabid animals, with specific mentions of outbreaks in Suffolk, Virginia; Mire, Louisiana; and Elmira, New York. Across July and August 2026, rabies-related inquiries rose by 17% compared to the same period in 2025. The agency also noted a 33% increase in rabies vaccine use and a 76% rise in immunoglobulin use. Health officials emphasized the importance of post-exposure prophylaxis (PEP) to prevent the virus from spreading to the central nervous system, as symptoms can begin with flu-like illnesses and progress to severe disease within weeks or months. The CDC warned that death is inevitable once symptoms appear, but PEP can prevent this. The agency also advised keeping pets up to date on rabies vaccines and avoiding contact with wildlife, especially those that are injured, sick, or dead. The CDC paused diagnostic testing for rabies earlier this year but resumed it by early September 2026.

analysis.event: Health officials reported an increase in human rabies exposures and mistakes in rabies treatments, as noted by the CDC. The CDC issued a Health Alert Network Health Advisory due to the recent uptick in rabies exposures and treatment errors.
analysis.scale_impact_and_risk: There were 17% more rabies-related inquiries in July and August 2026 compared to the previous year. A mass exposure event involved nearly 300 people exposed to rabies after interacting with goats at a mobile petting zoo. Three baby goats tested positive for rabies, and another was presumed rabid. analysis.location_and_population: In the United States, people are usually exposed to rabies by coming in contact with wild animals infected with the virus.
analysis.event: The CDC warns of an increase in animal rabies activity and human exposures.
analysis.scale_impact_and_risk: About 100,000 vaccinations due to potential rabies exposure in humans each year in the U.S. There are about 4,000 animal rabies cases reported each year, with 90% occurring in wild animals like bats, raccoons, skunks, and foxes.

analysis.brief_en: The CDC has warned of a rise in animal rabies activity and human exposures in the United States. Health officials advise vigilance and avoiding contact with sick-acting mammals and wildlife to prevent rabies transmission.
